subject: Colext - initial occupancy very high despite no detections

messages.author: 99a35bb737ac9f41
messages.subject: Colext - initial occupancy very high despite no detections
parts:
Dear all,

I am currently running dynamic occupancy models from camera trap data from 8 years over 64 sites and I am not sure I understand my results correctly.
For one of my study species, in the first year there was no detections at any of my locations. Only in the second year I got a first detection. After that the species started being detected more frequently as it is in the process of recolonizing our study area (as can be seen in the detection history). 


Now when I fit a model that includes covariates on the detection probability, the occupancy estimates obtained for each sites (using the smoothed estimates from the model output), are very high even in the first year and even for sites where the species was only first detected several years later. 


Could somebody explain to me why this is? Is there a problem with my model or is this normal? When I only use the null model without any covariates the estimates seem to be fine. I am posting my model output below.

Thank you very much!
Annika

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Colext - initial occupancy very high despite no detections
parts:
Dear Annika,

I don't think there is a problem, but perhaps modeling the detection component is challenging. Detection is the link between what you observe and what you infer is out there and thus is a critical component of such models.

Your output below suggests that detection probability is very close to zero at the intercept (plogis(-7.4)), and since the scaled year covariate has a strongly positive effect, p will be even smaller for year 1. Therefore, it seems that even without any detection in the first year, the estimates produced are such that high occupancy is a quite likely event.

Overall, I wonder whether this species may not simply be too rare for modeling, with just 0-4 observed detections in ~50 surveyed sites in any given year. In such a multi-species setting, a community occupancy model may be better, though you'd have to fit that with some Bayesian engine like JAGS.

Best regards  -- Marc
